2.3.3.1-f138.accuracy_reason: The lines are Epistles 1.16.75–77, and Horace does read 'saevo te sub custode tenebo', so the correction of the sidenote is right. The quoted Latin leaves out 'saevo' while the English keeps 'cruel', but this is minor.

2.3.3.1-f141.accuracy_reason: Horace reads 'simul atque volam, me solvet.' 'Opinor' begins the next sentence ('hoc sentit: moriar'), and the release meant there is death.

2.3.3.1-f148.accuracy_reason: Theocritus, Idyll 4.41–42 is Corydon comforting Battus ('tomorrow will be better; hope is for the living').

2.3.3.1-f151.accuracy_reason: The line is Horace, Epistles 1.4.14, not Ovid.

2.3.3.1-f154.accuracy_reason: This is the Latin form of the Greek proverb (πολλὰ μεταξὺ πέλει κύλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρου), and Burton does use it hopefully.

2.3.3.1-f155.accuracy_reason: Livy 39.26.9 has Philip V say 'nondum omnium dierum solem occidisse'.

2.3.3.1-f158.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 2 prose 4 reads 'infelicissimum genus infortunii est fuisse felicem'; the locus and sense are right.

2.3.3.1-f163.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Medea 176 is 'Fortuna opes auferre, non animum potest'; Burton's own sidenote quotes it, and here he gives it to Zeno in altered wording.

2.3.3.1-f165.accuracy_reason: Cicero, De officiis 1.38 quotes Ennius' Pyrrhus: 'Nec mi aurum posco nec mi pretium dederitis'; the context and variant are right.

2.3.3.1-f170.accuracy_reason: 'Rebus angustis animosus atque fortis appare' is Horace, Odes 2.10.21–22, so Burton's 'Od. 11' is a miscitation.

2.3.3.1-f173.accuracy_reason: The Enchiridion closes (ch. 53) with the Euripides verse saying that whoever yields well to necessity is wise; this matches Burton's sidenote to Epictetus.

2.3.3.1-f182.accuracy_reason: Seneca, De providentia 3.10 has Maecenas 'tam vigilabit in pluma quam ille [Regulus] in cruce', so Burton's wording closely condenses Seneca. The claim that it 'does not follow Seneca's text' overstates the difference.

2.3.3.1-f185.accuracy_reason: Pseudo-Sallust, Ad Caesarem senem 1.2, attributes 'fabrum esse suae quemque fortunae' to Appius (Claudius Caecus).

2.3.3.1-f186.accuracy_reason: Chrysostom wrote 'Quod nemo laeditur nisi a seipso'; the following English sentence renders Seneca, Ep. 98, as Burton's sidenote shows.

2.3.3.1-f188.accuracy_reason: The line is a sententia of Publilius Syrus ('Fortuna nimium quem fovet, stultum facit'), who was called Publius Mimus.

2.3.3.1-f196.accuracy_reason: De providentia 3.3 has Demetrius' 'nihil mihi videtur infelicius eo cui nihil umquam evenit adversi'.

2.3.3.1-f200.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 11.208 reads 'voluptates commendat rarior usus'; Burton adds 'quippe' and uses the singular.

2.3.3.1-f205.accuracy_reason: 'Dives' in Vulgate Luke 16:19 became the traditional name of the rich man.

2.3.3.1-f24.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.16.9–12 is correct, and Burton's verse does render the lictor as 'mayors' officers'.

2.3.3.1-f243.accuracy_reason: Horace, Odes 2.10.17–18 reads 'non, si male nunc, et olim / sic erit', so Burton has added 'semper'.

2.3.3.1-f244.accuracy_reason: Lucan, Pharsalia 5.527–529: the poet's apostrophe on the poor boatman Amyclas, whose hut Caesar visits at night.

2.3.3.1-f246.accuracy_reason: Ovid, Metamorphoses 3.466 reads 'inopem me copia fecit', spoken by Narcissus; Burton's version has 'se'.

2.3.3.1-f25.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.65 reads 'quid opus Cratero magnos promittere montis?' Craterus was a physician, and the note reads the sense correctly.

2.3.3.1-f250.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Ep. 90.10 reads 'culmus liberos texit, sub marmore atque auro servitus habitat'; Burton's changes are reported accurately.

2.3.3.1-f257.accuracy_reason: This is the end of the 'Duc me, O Jupiter, et tu Fatum' line of Cleanthes' prayer, which Epictetus quotes at the close of the Enchiridion.

2.3.3.1-f260.accuracy_reason: Gildas, De excidio 20, the 'groans of the Britons' to Aetius: 'repellunt barbari ad mare, repellit mare ad barbaros'.

2.3.3.1-f261.accuracy_reason: Diogenes Laertius 1.36: asked what was easy, Thales answered 'to give advice to another'.

2.3.3.1-f267.accuracy_reason: Tacitus, Histories 1.49 judges Galba 'capax imperii nisi imperasset', and Burton applies the formula to several emperors.

2.3.3.1-f27.accuracy_reason: The line numbers seem off by one: in standard editions 're veraque metus hominum' is 2.48, so the passage is 2.48–51, not 2.47–50. The variant readings given are correct.

2.3.3.1-f275.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Amos 6:4–6 is quoted correctly; Burton changes the second person to the third; 'Xenoph. Tyran.' is the Hiero; and of the three luxuries Burton's English gives only the ivory beds.

2.3.3.1-f277.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Georgics 2.506 does read 'ut gemma bibat et Sarrano dormiat ostro', and Sarra is the old name for Tyre. The note's account of Burton's changes (relative clause, indicative verbs, plural 'gemmis') is accurate.

2.3.3.1-f3.accuracy_reason: This is a scholastic maxim based on Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 1.5 (1095b), where honour depends more on those who give it than on the one who receives it. Burton's gloss 'honours are from God' does turn it towards God as the giver.

2.3.3.1-f33.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Thyestes 453 reads 'venenum in auro bibitur'. None of the nearby sidenotes credits Seneca.

2.3.3.1-f37.accuracy_reason: Juvenal 10.112–113 reads 'sine caede ac vulnere'. Burton has 'sanguine' instead. The glosses on Pluto and 'dry death' are right.

2.3.3.1-f38.accuracy_reason: The Vulgate of Isaiah 5:14 is quoted correctly, and Burton's wording is a loose adaptation of it.

2.3.3.1-f41.accuracy_reason: Virgil, Georgics 2.458 reads 'sua si bona norint, agricolas'. The note describes Burton's word order and his new application of the line correctly.

2.3.3.1-f49.accuracy_reason: In myth, the goat Amalthea nursed Jupiter, and her horn became the cornucopia.

2.3.3.1-f52.accuracy_reason: Horace, Epodes 2.1–3 does include 'ut prisca gens mortalium' as the middle line, and Burton leaves it out.

2.3.3.1-f61.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.2.133–135 reads 'dictus, erit nulli proprius, sed cedet in usum / nunc mihi, nunc alii'. The differences in Burton's text (erat, cedit, aliis) are reported correctly.

2.3.3.1-f63.accuracy_reason: Persius 3.72 reads 'humana qua parte locatus es in re'.

2.3.3.1-f70.accuracy_reason: Boethius, Consolation 2 m.5 reads 'Somnos dabat herba salubres, / potum quoque lubricus amnis'. The misprint and Burton's other changes are identified correctly.

2.3.3.1-f72.accuracy_reason: Lucretius 5.1118–1119 continues 'neque enim est umquam penuria parvi', which matches the note.

2.3.3.1-f75.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.65, the country suppers with friends at his Sabine farm.

2.3.3.1-f81.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.4–5 reads 'nil amplius oro, / Maia nate'. Mercury is the son of Maia.

2.3.3.1-f82.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.4.17–18 has 'finxerunt animi, raro et perpauca loquentis', as the note says.

2.3.3.1-f89.accuracy_reason: Cleanthes' hymn opens 'Lead me, O Zeus, and you, Destiny', and Epictetus quotes it at the close of the Enchiridion (ch. 53).

2.3.3.1-f91.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Thyestes 391–393, the chorus on the slippery heights of the court.

2.3.3.1-f94.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 2.6.1 reads 'modus agri non ita magnus', so Burton's 'parvus' reverses the sense. 'votiis' is plainly a misprint.

2.3.3.1-f98.accuracy_reason: Martial 10.47 is addressed to Julius Martialis. The omitted line is 'non ingratus ager, focus perennis', just before 'lis numquam'.

2.3.3.1-f99.accuracy_reason: Horace, Satires 1.1.92–94 runs 'parto quod avebas, ne facias quod / Ummidius quidam', so 'utere' is not Horace's.
